title: Ladder Logic: Reading Rungs
oneLiner: The visual language PLCs run instead of C# or Python -- contacts and coils wired between two rails, read left to right as "if these conditions are true, energize this output."
keyTakeaway: Series contacts = AND, parallel branches = OR, and a normally-closed contact = NOT -- ladder logic is the exact same boolean logic as Logic Gates, just drawn as an electrical circuit instead of gate symbols, because it replaced literal relay panels wired the same way.
explanation:
A ladder diagram is read like an actual electrical circuit: two vertical rails (power on the left, return on the right, by convention), and horizontal "rungs" between them, each ending in a COIL -- an output (a physical relay, an electrically operated switch, an indicator light, a motor starter, or in the PLC's internal logic, just a bit). A rung's coil energizes exactly when there's a complete conducting path from the left rail to it, through whatever CONTACTS sit in between -- which is precisely how the actual relay panels ladder logic replaced worked, wired with real wires and real relay contacts. This app's PLC scan cycle's "Execute Program" step (see PLCs: How They're Different From a Normal Computer) is running the equivalent of a diagram like this, top to bottom, rung by rung, every single scan.

Two contacts wired in SERIES (one after another on the same path) both have to be closed for current to reach the coil -- that's AND. Two contacts wired in PARALLEL (on separate branches that reconverge before the coil) only need ONE of them closed -- that's OR. And a contact can be drawn two ways: NORMALLY OPEN (conducts when its input is ON -- the usual case) or NORMALLY CLOSED (conducts when its input is OFF, and stops conducting the moment it turns ON -- inverted, easy to misread at a glance, and worth double-checking every time) -- that's a NOT. All three map directly onto Logic Gates' AND/OR/NOT, just drawn as a circuit instead of gate symbols.
